quote_json: "The unsafe features of C# are available only in unsafe contexts."
notes: 25.1 (PDF p. 335, line 24) makes the unsafe features available only in unsafe contexts, and 25.2 (PDF p. 337, line 42) admits pointer-type as a type only 'In an unsafe context'; the typeof clause 14.5.11 (PDF p. 165, lines 21-35) makes no exception. Outside an unsafe context the 1st edition's type grammar has no pointer-type (PDF p. 337 lines 9-10 and 42-46), so typeof(long*) in a safe Main is ill-formed; the leave to name a pointer type in typeof outside an unsafe context first appears in the 7th edition's 23.3 (PDF p. 577). Adding only 'unsafe' to Main makes the same expression valid (long is an unmanaged type, PDF p. 338 line 9), so the repair isolates the construct and nothing else in the program is at fault. Positive witnesses establish prerequisites; failing originals do not prove mutation sensitivity.

quote_json: "if E is classified as a volatile field"
notes: 25.5.4 (PDF p. 344, lines 17-21) says 'A compile-time error occurs if E is not classified as a variable, if E is classified as a volatile field (17.4.3), or if E denotes a moveable variable.' value.Flag is a fixed variable (25.3, PDF p. 340 lines 22-25), so only the volatile clause applies; an int volatile field is allowed (17.4.3, PDF p. 240 lines 9-13), removing only 'volatile' repairs it, and the 7th edition replaced the clause with a read-only-local ban (23.6.5, PDF p. 586). A warning is 'an informational message ... intended to identify a potentially questionable usage' (PDF p. 22 lines 20-21), not the compile-time error the clause requires (PDF p. 21 line 42). The only counter-text is clause 2's general leave to compile a diagnosed extension (PDF p. 17 lines 36-40), which would excuse any warning-only acceptance anywhere in the suite, so it does not make this rule ambiguous. Positive witnesses establish prerequisites; failing originals do not prove mutation sensitivity.
